messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At seventy-two, Amara Vance still feels the weight of those years in the highlands, though she has lived in Ohio for more than four decades. She was twenty-four when the borders collapsed, and she was caught in the siege that turned her village into a grid of rubble and smoke. The men with rifles moved with the precision of hunters, and Amara learned quickly that stillness was a death sentence. She remembers the afternoon the shelling began, the way the earth heaved beneath her feet, and how the concussive blasts rattled her teeth long after the ground stopped shaking. Darkness was never empty back then; it was a curtain pulled over ambushes, and she watched from a collapsed cellar as figures emerged from the treeline, their shadows stretching long and silent across the dirt. That siege did not end with a treaty so much as a quiet retreat, but it left an indelible blueprint in her nervous system. Amara had come to believe that the world was fundamentally untrustworthy, that safety was an illusion maintained only by constant readiness. Since her husband passed five years ago, the silence of her own home has grown heavy, leaving her alone with the memories that never fade. When she eventually took up forestry work in the state woodlands, Amara found herself mapping the quiet landscape against the trauma of those years. She spent her days walking dense tracts of pine and hardwood, but the isolation slowly bred a different kind of tension. To manage the unease, she developed a routine of constant vigilance. She made a practice of scanning the horizon every few minutes, noting footprints in the mud or the way a colleague’s uniform hung on a frame, her eyes never resting on one spot for long. This relentless checking kept her shoulders knotted and her breath shallow. She was certain that lowering her guard would invite disaster, so she told herself it was just professional caution. But because she kept her body locked in a state of perpetual readiness, her nervous system stopped distinguishing between a falling branch and a sudden detonation. She would crank up her truck radio or blast the television in her cabin to drown out the silence, a sensory distraction that offered only temporary relief before the static itself began to trigger a flinch. The more she checked the tree lines and the more she amplified noise to control her surroundings, the more fragile her peace became. These habits actually sharpened her sensitivity to danger, so that when a distant thunderclap rolled over the pines, her body reacted as though mortars were falling again. The loud music and the frantic scanning did not calm her; they kept her on high alert, ensuring that every shadow and every sudden sound registered as an immediate, life-threatening alarm. Over the years, this cycle had carved a narrow path through her work and her days. She stopped attending the monthly ranger gatherings, convincing herself she was too busy with inventory, though crowded rooms made her palms sweat and her head throb. Last autumn, when a backhoe engine backfired and she had fled her truck into the deep woods, hiding beneath a fallen log until her breathing steadied, she finally recognized that the precautions she had clung to for decades were no longer protecting her. What frightened her most was the realization that the hyper-vigilance and the noise she used to buffer herself were actually holding her captive, amplifying the very alarms she was trying to silence. Amara walked into the clinic today carrying a worn leather journal and a quiet desperation. She had come to understand that she needed a different way to navigate the quiet. What she most hoped for was simply to sleep through the night without waking to check the door, and to walk the forest floor again without waiting for the next threat to materialize.
